def: A spoken or written account of connected events; a story.
ex: The documentary constructs a compelling narrative about the rise of renewable energy sources.
nat: Changing the public narrative requires consistent communication from leadership.

mis.bad: He told an interesting narrative yesterday.
mis.good: He shared a compelling narrative yesterday.
mis.why: In everyday speech, prefer "story" for informal tales; "narrative" fits structured or cultural accounts.

def: To become less wide or to reduce the number of possibilities or choices.
ex: We must narrow our list of candidates down to three finalists by tomorrow.
nat: The mountain road narrows sharply after the second bridge.

mis.bad: We need to narrow down on the choices.
mis.good: We need to narrow down the choices.
mis.why: Use "narrow down + object" without the preposition "on".

def: Highly unpleasant, unkind, malicious, or dangerous in nature.
ex: He caught a nasty virus that kept him in bed for an entire week.
nat: Try to avoid nasty comments during heated team discussions.

mis.bad: He was nasty with his coworkers.
mis.good: He was nasty to his coworkers.
mis.why: Say someone is "nasty to" people, not "with".

def: To plan and direct the route of travel, or successfully manage a complex situation.
ex: New employees often find it challenging to navigate company bureaucracy without proper mentorship.
nat: Use the mobile app to navigate the underground train network smoothly.

mis.bad: I navigated on the city using my phone.
mis.good: I navigated the city using my phone.
mis.why: "Navigate" is transitive when referring to exploring a place or system; drop "on".

def: In a tidy, orderly, or carefully arranged manner.
ex: She neatly stacked all the project folders in chronological order before leaving.
nat: The data points are neatly summarized in the final chapter.

mis.bad: He organized the files very neatly and careful.
mis.good: He organized the files very neatly and carefully.
mis.why: Coordinate adverbs with adverbs: "neatly and carefully".

def: To make something necessary as a result or consequence.
ex: The sudden increase in user traffic will necessitate upgrading our cloud infrastructure.
nat: Severe storm damage will necessitate major structural repairs next week.

mis.bad: The crisis necessitated to hire consultants.
mis.good: The crisis necessitated hiring consultants.
mis.why: "Necessitate" takes a direct object or gerund (-ing), never "to + infinitive".

def: Done or occurring without necessity; completely avoidable and unnecessary.
ex: Automating routine reports saved the engineering team hours of needless manual effort.
nat: Needless to say, we must test everything thoroughly before launch.

mis.bad: Needless of say, we agreed.
mis.good: Needless to say, we agreed.
mis.why: The fixed idiom is always "needless to say", never "of say".

def: To fail to care for properly, or fail to do something necessary.
ex: You should never neglect routine maintenance on production databases or server backups.
nat: He neglected his health while working eighty hours a week.

mis.bad: She neglected from doing her homework.
mis.good: She neglected to do her homework.
mis.why: Use "neglect to do something", not "neglect from doing".

def: Failure to take proper care in doing something, often resulting in damage.
ex: The court ruled that company negligence caused the massive confidential data leak.
nat: Medical negligence can carry severe legal and financial penalties for hospitals.

mis.bad: The incident happened by negligence of him.
mis.good: The incident happened due to his negligence.
mis.why: Say "due to / because of his negligence", not "by negligence of him".

def: So small or unimportant as to be not worth considering.
ex: The performance impact of adding one more analytics tag was completely negligible.
nat: The difference in flight ticket prices between airlines was virtually negligible.

mis.bad: The cost was very negligible to mention.
mis.good: The cost was negligible, so we ignored it.
mis.why: "Negligible" is an absolute descriptor meaning practically zero; avoid "very negligible".

def: Causing severe stress, tension, or anxiety.
ex: Delivering your very first technical presentation in English is always nerve-racking.
nat: Waiting for the medical test results proved to be a nerve-racking experience.

mis.bad: The interview was very nerve-breaking.
mis.good: The interview was nerve-racking.
mis.why: The idiom is "nerve-racking" (or "nerve-wracking"), not "nerve-breaking".

def: A structure built by birds or animals to hold eggs, or a snug retreat.
ex: A pair of swallows built a mud nest right above our front doorway.
nat: They saved money diligently to build a cozy nest for their retirement.

mis.bad: The bird made its ninho on the roof.
mis.good: The bird built its nest on the roof.
mis.why: Remember "nest" is the English word for "ninho", with "build" as common verb.

def: Not supporting or helping either side in a conflict or disagreement; impartial.
ex: The mediator maintained a completely neutral tone throughout the intense contract dispute.
nat: Choose neutral colors like beige or gray for your home office walls.

mis.bad: He stayed neutral to both opinions.
mis.good: He remained neutral on both issues.
mis.why: Use "neutral on/about an issue" or "remain neutral toward parties".

def: The state of not supporting or helping either side in a dispute or war.
ex: The country declared strict neutrality during the conflict to protect international trade.
nat: Network neutrality ensures internet providers treat all data packets equally.

mis.bad: They proved their neutralness in the debate.
mis.good: They demonstrated their neutrality in the debate.
mis.why: The standard noun is "neutrality", not "neutralness".

def: To render something ineffective or harmless by applying an opposite force.
ex: Security teams moved fast to neutralize the malicious malware payload before execution.
nat: Add baking soda to the vinegar mixture to neutralize excess acid.

mis.bad: The patch neutralized against the virus.
mis.good: The patch neutralized the threat.
mis.why: "Neutralize" is transitive; do not insert "against".

def: A person who has recently arrived in a place or joined an activity.
ex: The mentor organized weekly lunch sessions to help every newcomer settle in comfortably.
nat: The startup is a relative newcomer in the competitive fintech market.

mis.bad: He is a new comer on the company.
mis.good: He is a newcomer to the company.
mis.why: "Newcomer" is written as one word and takes the preposition "to".

def: Recently, or in a new or different way.
ex: The newly appointed director scheduled one-on-one meetings with every team member.
nat: We moved into a newly renovated apartment near the city center.

mis.bad: They are new married couple.
mis.good: They are a newly married couple.
mis.why: Use the adverb "newly" to modify past participles like "married" or "appointed".

def: The time between evening and morning; the period of darkness.
ex: Street lighting was improved to make nighttime walking much safer for residents.
nat: Owls are predators that hunt predominantly during the nighttime hours.

mis.bad: I prefer studying in the night time.
mis.good: I prefer studying during the nighttime.
mis.why: "Nighttime" is usually a single word or used attributively as "nighttime hours".

def: Zero, especially as a score in sports matches, or nothing at all.
ex: The chances of recovering the corrupted database without backups were virtually nil.
nat: Arsenal defeated their rivals by three goals to nil in London.

mis.bad: Our budget for marketing is zero to nil.
mis.good: Our chances of failure are virtually nil.
mis.why: Use "nil" for sports scores ("two-nil") or fixed idioms ("virtually nil").

def: Quick and light in movement or action; agile in thinking.
ex: Small agile teams remain nimble enough to pivot quickly when user needs change.
nat: Her nimble fingers moved across the piano keys with remarkable precision.

mis.bad: He has a very nimbler mind.
mis.good: He has a very nimble mind.
mis.why: Do not use comparative "-er" after "very"; say "very nimble".

def: A member of a people with no permanent home, or a digital traveler.
ex: Working as a digital nomad allowed him to explore twelve different countries last year.
nat: Traditional pastoral nomads move livestock across seasonal mountain grazing pastures.

mis.bad: He lives like an nomad in Europe.
mis.good: He lives like a nomad in Europe.
mis.why: Use the indefinite article "a" because "nomad" begins with a consonant sound /n/.

def: Living the life of a nomad; wandering from place to place.
ex: Many remote tech workers adopt a nomadic lifestyle while working across time zones.
nat: Nomadic tribes have inhabited these arid desert regions for thousands of years.

mis.bad: She leads a nomadic life style.
mis.good: She leads a nomadic lifestyle.
mis.why: Write "lifestyle" as one compound word.

def: Existing in name only, or very small compared to the expected cost.
ex: The museum charges a nominal admission fee of two dollars for university students.
nat: The Queen remains the nominal head of state in several Commonwealth nations.

mis.bad: We paid a nominal price very cheap.
mis.good: We paid a nominal fee for entrance.
mis.why: "Nominal" already means insignificantly small in price; drop redundant words like "very cheap".

def: To propose formally that someone should be chosen for an honor or position.
ex: The committee will nominate three senior engineers for the annual innovation award.
nat: Members can nominate any qualified colleague before the voting deadline on Friday.

mis.bad: They nominated him to win the prize.
mis.good: They nominated him for the prize.
mis.why: Use "nominate someone for [an award/position]", not "to win".

def: The act of officially suggesting someone for an election, job, or honor.
ex: Her nomination for best lead architect was enthusiastically celebrated across the whole company.
nat: The Academy announced the final list of award nominations yesterday afternoon.

mis.bad: She won a nomination for the Oscar.
mis.good: She received an Oscar nomination.
mis.why: You "receive" or "earn" a nomination; you do not "win" a nomination itself.

def: Not conducted or maintained for the purpose of making a profit.
ex: She left corporate banking to manage finances for an educational non-profit foundation.
nat: The non-profit clinic offers free medical checkups to low-income local families.

mis.bad: He works in a non-lucrative institution.
mis.good: He works at a non-profit organization.
mis.why: Brazilian learners often calque "não lucrativo" as "non-lucrative"; use "non-profit".

def: Without making any stops or interruptions along the way.
ex: Our flight flew nonstop from São Paulo all the way to Frankfurt.
nat: The engineering team worked nonstop through the weekend to patch the leak.

mis.bad: The airplane flew in non-stop.
mis.good: The plane flew nonstop.
mis.why: Use "nonstop" directly as an adverb; do not add the preposition "in".

def: The process of bringing something back to a normal or standardized condition.
ex: Database normalization eliminates redundant data columns and prevents unexpected insertion anomalies.
nat: Both governments welcomed the gradual normalization of bilateral diplomatic relations.

mis.bad: The normalisation of relations took months.
mis.good: The normalization of relations took months.
mis.why: American English spelling prefers "normalization" with a "z".

def: A sentimental longing or wistful affection for the past.
ex: Listening to classic video game soundtracks always fills me with pleasant childhood nostalgia.
nat: The vintage clothing exhibition triggered immense nostalgia among older visitors.

mis.bad: I feel nostalgia of my school days.
mis.good: I feel nostalgia for my school days.
mis.why: Use "nostalgia for [a time/place]", never "of".

def: Worthy of attention or notice; remarkable or prominent.
ex: The latest software release introduced several notable improvements to overall battery life.
nat: A notable exception to the general company rule was the design department.

mis.bad: He is a notable person in the city.
mis.good: He is a prominent figure in the city.
mis.why: "Notable" most often describes features, events, or achievements rather than people.

def: In a way that is especially worth noting; particularly or significantly.
ex: Several European countries, most notably Germany, have invested heavily in wind turbines.
nat: The interface has improved notably since the last major update in March.

mis.bad: Many tools failed, notably being the old compiler.
mis.good: Many tools failed, most notably the old compiler.
mis.why: Use "most notably + noun phrase" directly without adding auxiliary verbs like "being".

def: Deserving attention because of being important, interesting, or significant.
ex: One noteworthy detail from the audit was the complete lack of external dependencies.
nat: The researcher published several noteworthy papers on artificial neural networks this year.

mis.bad: It is a note-worthy point for discuss.
mis.good: It is a noteworthy point to discuss.
mis.why: "Noteworthy" is written as one word without a hyphen, followed by "to + verb".

def: To inform someone of something, typically in a formal or official way.
ex: The automated monitor will immediately notify the on-call engineer when latency spikes.
nat: Tenants must notify the landlord at least thirty days before moving out.

mis.bad: Please notify about the incident.
mis.good: Please notify the manager about the incident.
mis.why: "Notify" requires a direct personal object: "notify someone about something".

def: A general conception, idea, or belief about something.
ex: Modern neuroscience rejects the outdated notion that adult brains cannot generate new connections.
nat: She had no notion of how much effort the migration would require.

mis.bad: I have no notion about what happened.
mis.good: I have no idea what happened.
mis.why: In informal contexts, use "no idea"; "notion" is more philosophical or theoretical.

def: Famous or well known, typically for some bad quality or deed.
ex: The old legacy billing codebase was notorious among developers for unexpected race conditions.
nat: That intersection is notorious for severe traffic accidents during rainy evening hours.

mis.bad: He is a notorious scientist who won awards.
mis.good: He is a renowned scientist who won awards.
mis.why: False friend alert: "notorious" in English always has a negative connotation; use "renowned" for positive fame.

def: To provide with the substances necessary for growth, health, and good condition.
ex: Fresh leafy vegetables and whole foods nourish the body far better than supplements.
nat: Reading widely helps nourish your creativity and problem-solving skills as an engineer.

mis.bad: Good food nourishes to your health.
mis.good: Good food nourishes your body.
mis.why: "Nourish" is a transitive verb; do not add "to" after it.

def: The food or other substances necessary for growth, health, and good condition.
ex: Healthy seeds and nuts provide essential nourishment during long strenuous mountain treks.
nat: Artistic expression offers deep spiritual nourishment during emotionally demanding life chapters.

mis.bad: Babies need much nourishments to grow.
mis.good: Babies need adequate nourishment to grow.
mis.why: "Nourishment" is uncountable; do not use it in the plural form.

def: A person new to or inexperienced in a field, trade, or situation.
ex: The tutorial is thoughtfully designed so that even a complete novice can deploy.
nat: As a novice chess player, he studied basic opening principles every evening.

mis.bad: He is a novice in programming languages.
mis.good: He is a novice at programming.
mis.why: Use "novice at [an activity]" or use it directly as a noun adjunct ("novice coder").

def: A person, thing, or circumstance causing inconvenience or mild annoyance.
ex: Filling out paper travel reimbursement forms by hand was an absolute nuisance for everyone.
nat: Loud construction noise next door became a daily nuisance for remote workers.

mis.bad: The spam emails make a nuisance to me.
mis.good: The spam emails are a real nuisance.
mis.why: Say something "is a nuisance", not "makes a nuisance to me".

def: To make legally null and void; to invalidate or make of no value.
ex: Signing the amended contract will effectively nullify all previous informal email agreements.
nat: A critical syntax error in the configuration file can nullify your security rules.

mis.bad: The judge nullified off the contract.
mis.good: The judge nullified the contract.
mis.why: Do not add "off" or "out" to "nullify"; it is directly transitive.

def: Deprived of the power of sensation, feeling, or movement.
ex: Walking outside in freezing temperatures without gloves left my fingertips completely numb.
nat: She felt numb with shock after hearing the sudden restructuring announcement.

mis.bad: My hands were numbed from the cold.
mis.good: My hands were numb from the cold.
mis.why: Use the adjective "numb" to describe state, not the past participle "numbed".

def: The state of being unable to feel sensation in a part of your body.
ex: Typing for hours without ergonomic wrist support caused recurring numbness in his right hand.
nat: The patient reported numbness spreading from her lower back down into her leg.

mis.bad: I felt a numbness in my hand.
mis.good: I felt numbness in my hand.
mis.why: "Numbness" is generally uncountable when referring to physical sensation; omit the article "a".

def: Relating to, consisting of, or expressed in numbers.
ex: Please enter a six-digit numeric password without letters or special characters.
nat: The function validates that user input contains only numeric values before saving.

mis.bad: Provide your numbers password.
mis.good: Provide your numeric password.
mis.why: Use the adjective "numeric" or "numerical" rather than the noun "numbers".

def: To care for and encourage the growth or development of someone or something.
ex: Great tech managers nurture young talent by assigning challenging projects with safety nets.
nat: We must nurture strong collaborative relationships between product designers and frontend developers.

mis.bad: The company nurtures on internal talent.
mis.good: The company nurtures internal talent.
mis.why: "Nurture" is a direct transitive verb; omit prepositions like "on" or "for".

def: Used in the phrase "in a nutshell" to mean in the fewest possible words.
ex: In a nutshell, our proposal cuts server running costs in half without hurting performance.
nat: To put it in a nutshell, the merger was approved unanimously.

mis.bad: Inside a nutshell, the plan worked.
mis.good: In a nutshell, the plan worked.
mis.why: The fixed English idiom is always "in a nutshell", never "inside a nutshell".

def: An act or course of action to which a person is morally or legally bound.
ex: Tenants have a legal obligation to report plumbing leaks promptly to building management.
nat: He felt no moral obligation to reply to unsolicited commercial sales messages.

mis.bad: I have the obligation of finish this report.
mis.good: I have an obligation to finish this report.
mis.why: Use "obligation to + verb", not "obligation of + verb".

def: Required by a legal, moral, or other rule; compulsory.
ex: Wearing safety goggles is strictly obligatory when entering the chemical engineering laboratory.
nat: Attending the Monday sprint retrospective is obligatory for all active team members.

mis.bad: It is obligatory of attend the meeting.
mis.good: It is obligatory to attend the meeting.
mis.why: Say "it is obligatory to do something", not "of attend".

def: To make someone legally or morally bound to do something, or to do a favor for someone.
ex: The signed contract obliges the software vendor to deliver quarterly feature updates.
nat: If you need a quiet workspace, I will gladly oblige by booking room four.

mis.bad: The law obliges to report the incident.
mis.good: The law obliges companies to report the incident.
mis.why: When "oblige" means compel, use "oblige someone to do something".

pt: obscuro / pouco conhecido / difícil de entender
def: Not discovered or known about; uncertain or difficult to understand.
ex: The library crashed because of an obscure bug deep inside the legacy crypto module.
nat: He quoted an obscure Latin phrase that nobody at the meeting understood.

mis.bad: The reason is very obscurity.
mis.good: The reason is very obscure.
mis.why: Use the adjective "obscure" after "is", not the noun "obscurity".

def: The state of being unknown, inconspicuous, or difficult to comprehend.
ex: The indie band rose from complete obscurity to international fame in six months.
nat: Excessive academic jargon often clouds the topic in unnecessary technical obscurity.

mis.bad: He lived in the obscurity.
mis.good: He lived in obscurity.
mis.why: The idiom is "live in obscurity" without the definite article "the".

def: Quick to notice things; paying careful attention to details.
ex: An observant quality assurance engineer noticed the intermittent race condition during manual testing.
nat: He was observant enough to realize she felt uncomfortable in the crowded room.

mis.bad: He is very observer with small bugs.
mis.good: He is very observant of small bugs.
mis.why: Use the adjective "observant" rather than the noun "observer" to describe a watchful person.

def: The practice of obeying a law or rule, or following a custom.
ex: Strict observance of regional data privacy regulations protects customer records from unauthorized exposure.
nat: The national holiday includes the observance of a solemn moment of silence.

mis.bad: The observance with the rules is mandatory.
mis.good: Strict observance of the rules is mandatory.
mis.why: Say "observance of rules", not "observance with".

def: To continually think about something to an unreasonable or troubling degree.
ex: It is easy to obsess over micro-benchmarks instead of writing clear and readable code.
nat: Do not obsess about minor grammatical mistakes when practicing your daily speaking fluency.

mis.bad: He obsesses with the website traffic.
mis.good: He obsesses over website traffic.
mis.why: Use "obsess over" or "obsess about", not "obsess with".

def: Thinking about something so much that you cannot think of anything else.
ex: Her obsessive attention to clean typography made the product documentation extremely pleasant to read.
nat: Checking work email late every night can quickly become an unhealthy obsessive habit.

mis.bad: He has an obsessive about clean code.
mis.good: He has an obsessive focus on clean code.
mis.why: "Obsessive" is an adjective; use "obsession" as the noun.

def: An idea or thought that continually preoccupies or intrudes on someone's mind.
ex: His obsession with system latency pushed the team to shave another fifty milliseconds off.
nat: Coffee roasting turned from a casual weekend hobby into a lifelong creative obsession.

mis.bad: She has an obsession by cleanliness.
mis.good: She has an obsession with cleanliness.
mis.why: Always use "obsession with [something]", never "by".

def: To get, acquire, or secure something through effort or formal request.
ex: International remote consultants must obtain a special commercial work permit before billing clients.
nat: We were unable to obtain permission to film inside the historic royal palace.

mis.bad: I obtained a very nice t-shirt.
mis.good: I bought a very nice t-shirt.
mis.why: "Obtain" is formal; for everyday purchases, prefer "buy", "get", or "pick up".

def: Able to be obtained, achieved, or acquired with reasonable effort.
ex: Setting ambitious yet obtainable sprint milestones keeps the engineering team motivated without burning out.
nat: Detailed customer usage reports are easily obtainable through the unified analytics dashboard.

mis.bad: The files are not obtainable for download.
mis.good: The files are not available for download.
mis.why: For downloads or web assets, "available" is much more idiomatic than "obtainable".

def: A person who resides in, uses, or is inside a particular space.
ex: Every single vehicle occupant was safely evacuated before emergency firefighters reached the scene.
nat: The previous occupant left a detailed manual explaining how the boiler system works.

mis.bad: The occupants of the room was shouting.
mis.good: The occupants of the room were shouting.
mis.why: Remember "occupants" is plural and requires a plural verb ("were").

def: To fill, exist in, or take up a space, time, or attention.
ex: Administrative meetings occupy nearly thirty percent of our working hours every single week.
nat: Solving technical architecture puzzles continues to occupy my thoughts during morning train commutes.

mis.bad: The table is occupated right now.
mis.good: The table is occupied right now.
mis.why: The past participle and adjective is "occupied", not "occupated".

def: An incident or event; or the fact or frequency of something happening.
ex: Microservice network timeouts were a daily occurrence before the new load balancer deployment.
nat: Flooding along the coastal highway is now a frequent occurrence during winter storms.

mis.bad: This error is a common ocurrence here.
mis.good: This error is a common occurrence here.
mis.why: Note the double "c" and double "r": "occurrence".

def: Different from what is usual or expected; or an integer not divisible by two.
ex: I noticed an odd sound coming from the laptop fan whenever compiling code.
nat: Three and five are prime examples of positive odd numbers in mathematics.

mis.bad: It is an odd number: four.
mis.good: It is an even number: four.
mis.why: Do not confuse "odd" (ímpar) with "even" (par).

def: The chances or likelihood of something happening or being the case.
ex: Against all odds, the bootstrapped mobile startup achieved profitability in its very first year.
nat: What are the odds that our transatlantic flight departs on time despite fog?

mis.bad: The odds is very high.
mis.good: The odds are very high.
mis.why: "Odds" is grammatically plural and takes a plural verb: "the odds are".

def: A person who commits an illegal act, or something responsible for a problem.
ex: Unoptimized images were the worst offender when analyzing mobile web page loading speeds.
nat: Community rehabilitation programs aim to prevent young offenders from committing further crimes.

mis.bad: He was an offender of the contract.
mis.good: He breached the contract.
mis.why: In legal business contexts, use "breach a contract" rather than call someone an "offender of".

def: A breach of a law or rule; an illegal act; or feeling hurt.
ex: Driving above the speed limit in a school zone is considered a serious offense.
nat: No offense intended, but your proposed design needs much stronger visual contrast.

mis.bad: I took offense about his remark.
mis.good: I took offense at his remark.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "take offense at [something]", not "about".

def: Causing someone to feel deeply hurt, upset, or angry; insulting.
ex: The platform quickly banned the user account for posting openly offensive and hateful comments.
nat: Rotting waste left outside the restaurant created an overwhelmingly offensive chemical smell.

mis.bad: I felt offensive by his joke.
mis.good: I felt offended by his joke.
mis.why: Use "-ed" for how you feel ("offended") and "-ive" for the thing causing it ("offensive joke").

def: Someone or something that has been left out or excluded, intentionally or not.
ex: The technical editor spotted a critical omission in the database migration recovery guide.
nat: Leaving his name off the list of project contributors was a glaring omission.

mis.bad: It was an omission from the part of management.
mis.good: It was an oversight on the part of management.
mis.why: Say "on the part of [someone]", not "from the part of".

def: Not able to be seen through; or difficult to understand or explain.
ex: The pricing policy for enterprise clients remained completely opaque and lacked clear guidelines.
nat: Frost on the bathroom window rendered the glass panel entirely opaque to outsiders.

mis.bad: The explanation was very opaquely.
mis.good: The explanation was very opaque.
mis.why: Use the adjective "opaque" after linking verbs like "was", not the adverb.

def: Without concealment, deception, or pretense; frankly and publicly.
ex: Team members are encouraged to speak openly about architectural doubts during daily standups.
nat: She openly acknowledged that the initial product deadline had been overly optimistic.

mis.bad: He talked in open about his feelings.
mis.good: He spoke openly about his feelings.
mis.why: Use the adverb "openly", not the literal Portuguese translation "in open".

def: To function or cause to function, or manage a business system.
ex: The payment processing system will operate normally during the upcoming scheduled network maintenance.
nat: Surgeons had to operate immediately to repair the athlete torn knee ligament.

mis.bad: The machine operates with battery.
mis.good: The machine operates on batteries.
mis.why: Machines or devices "operate on" a power source or fuel, not "with".

def: In or ready for use; or relating to the operation of something.
ex: The new backup data center will become fully operational by the end of October.
nat: Weekly meetings focus strictly on operational challenges rather than long-term product vision.

mis.bad: The server is already operatingly.
mis.good: The server is already operational.
mis.why: Use the adjective "operational" after the linking verb "is".

def: Functioning or having effect; or most significant or relevant.
ex: In that legal contract clause, the operative word is "may" rather than "shall".
nat: The new safety policy becomes operative starting the first Monday of next month.

mis.bad: The law became operative from five days.
mis.good: The law became operative five days ago.
mis.why: Say "became operative [time] ago" or "becomes operative on [date]".

def: Someone who competes with or opposes another in a contest or debate.
ex: The debate champion shook hands with her opponent before taking her seat.
nat: He respected his political opponent despite holding fundamentally conflicting economic opinions.

mis.bad: He was my apponent in the match.
mis.good: He was my opponent in the match.
mis.why: Spell "opponent" with an "o" at the beginning, not an "a".

def: Done or occurring at a well-chosen or particularly favorable time.
ex: The unexpected funding grant arrived at a very opportune moment for the struggling lab.
nat: It was an opportune time to launch our remote collaboration tool worldwide.

mis.bad: He arrived in an opportunity moment.
mis.good: He arrived at an opportune moment.
mis.why: Use the adjective "opportune" to modify "moment", not the noun "opportunity".

def: A person who takes advantage of opportunities as they arise, regardless of principle.
ex: Critics labeled the politician an unprincipled opportunist who switched parties whenever polling dipped.
nat: The market crash attracted financial opportunists eager to buy distressed physical properties.

mis.bad: He is very oportunist.
mis.good: He is very opportunistic / an opportunist.
mis.why: Use the adjective "opportunistic" or the noun phrase "an opportunist".

def: To keep someone in subservience and hardship, especially by the unjust exercise of authority.
ex: Authoritarian governments oppress free journalists by censoring news and threatening jail time.
nat: High taxes and heavy debt can oppress small local businesses for decades.

mis.bad: The dictator oppressed against the people.
mis.good: The dictator oppressed the people.
mis.why: "Oppress" is a transitive verb; do not add "against".

def: Inflicting harsh and authoritarian treatment, or weather that is uncomfortably hot and humid.
ex: Walking through downtown Manaus at noon can be difficult due to oppressive tropical humidity.
nat: Employees felt anxious working under the manager overly oppressive and micromanaging regime.

mis.bad: The heat was very oppressant.
mis.good: The heat was oppressive.
mis.why: The English adjective is "oppressive", not "oppressant".

def: Best or most favorable; optimum.
ex: Eight hours of restful sleep is considered optimal for memory retention and recovery.
nat: We tuned the caching layer to achieve optimal performance during sudden traffic surges.

mis.bad: This is the most optimal way to do it.
mis.good: This is the optimal way to do it.
mis.why: "Optimal" already means the best possible; do not say "most optimal".

def: Hopefulness and confidence about the future or the success of something.
ex: Despite market turbulence, international investors expressed cautious optimism about emerging technology stocks.
nat: Her infectious optimism energized the entire engineering team during a difficult release.

mis.bad: I have optimism on the new project.
mis.good: I feel optimism about the new project.
mis.why: Express optimism "about" something, not "on".

def: Available to be chosen but not obligatory.
ex: Adding profile photos on the community forum is completely optional for all registered members.
nat: The course includes four optional workshops on advanced distributed systems design.

mis.bad: The attendance is optic.
mis.good: Attendance is optional.
mis.why: Do not confuse "optional" (facultativo) with "optical" (visual/óptico).

def: Spoken rather than written; relating to the mouth.
ex: Candidates must pass both a written code challenge and an oral interview round.
nat: Maintaining good oral hygiene reduces the risk of serious long-term dental problems.

mis.bad: He gave an oral testimony written.
mis.good: He gave spoken testimony.
mis.why: "Oral" means spoken by mouth; do not combine it with "written".

def: Neatly and methodically arranged; peaceful and well-behaved.
ex: Passengers evacuated the stalled subway train in a remarkably calm and orderly fashion.
nat: Keep your local git commit history clean and orderly before opening a pull request.

mis.bad: They walked very orderly down the hall.
mis.good: They walked in an orderly manner down the hall.
mis.why: "Orderly" is an adjective, not an adverb; use "in an orderly manner".

def: With no special or distinctive features; normal and usual.
ex: It looked like an ordinary email, but it contained a sophisticated phishing payload.
nat: Ordinary citizens should not bear the financial cost of corporate environmental misconduct.

mis.bad: He is an ordinary man (meaning vulgar).
mis.good: He is a common / vulgar man.
mis.why: In Portuguese "ordinário" often means rude or vulgar; in English "ordinary" simply means normal or average.

def: To have a specified beginning or source; to create or initiate.
ex: Modern jazz styles originate largely from traditional African rhythms brought to New Orleans.
nat: The suspicious network traffic appeared to originate from a server in Eastern Europe.

mis.bad: The idea originated of a conversation.
mis.good: The idea originated from a conversation.
mis.why: Use "originate from [a source]" or "originate in [a place]", never "of".

def: A thing used to make something look more attractive but having no practical purpose.
ex: Handmade glass ornaments decorated the tall Christmas tree inside the historic hotel lobby.
nat: She viewed the expensive ceramic sculpture purely as an aesthetic ornament for the shelf.

mis.bad: We bought many ornaments to decorate.
mis.good: We bought ornaments for decoration.
mis.why: Say "ornaments for decoration", or simply "decorations".

def: Conforming to what is generally or traditionally accepted as right or true.
ex: His innovative investment strategy defied orthodox economic theories about diversification and index funds.
nat: They follow orthodox practices and keep a strictly kosher kitchen at home.

mis.bad: His approach was very orthodoxal.
mis.good: His approach was very orthodox.
mis.why: The English adjective is "orthodox", not "orthodoxal".

def: To move or swing back and forth at a regular speed, or waver between opinions.
ex: Stock prices oscillate wildly whenever the central bank hints at possible interest rate hikes.
nat: He tended to oscillate between unbridled enthusiasm and profound self-doubt before major presentations.

mis.bad: The price oscillated around fifty to sixty.
mis.good: The price oscillated between fifty and sixty.
mis.why: Use "oscillate between X and Y" when naming two endpoints.

def: A person who has been rejected by society or a social group.
ex: Blowing the whistle on company fraud turned him into an outcast among former executives.
nat: The protagonist in the novel felt like a social outcast throughout secondary school.

mis.bad: He was transformed in an outcast.
mis.good: He was turned into an outcast.
mis.why: Use "turned into an outcast", not "transformed in".

def: An exclamation or shout of public disagreement, anger, or strong protest.
ex: There was a massive public outcry after the municipality decided to bulldoze the park.
nat: The proposed security surveillance bill sparked immediate outcry from civil liberties advocacy groups.

mis.bad: There was an outcry of the public.
mis.good: There was a public outcry.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "public outcry" instead of "outcry of the public".

def: To be more successful or better than someone else at doing something.
ex: The younger sibling always strived to outdo her older brother in academic competitions.
nat: Each tech giant attempted to outdo the other by announcing newer artificial intelligence tools.

mis.bad: He outdid with his rivals.
mis.good: He outdid his rivals.
mis.why: "Outdo" is directly transitive; do not insert "with".

pt: tomada elétrica / ponto de venda / canal de desabafo
def: A power socket, a store selling goods, or a means of releasing emotion.
ex: Remember to bring an electrical adapter because British wall outlets use three rectangular pins.
nat: Long-distance running served as an essential psychological outlet during months of heavy project stress.

mis.bad: I need to plug in the tomada.
mis.good: I need to plug it into the wall outlet.
mis.why: Remember "wall outlet" (or "socket") is the English term for "tomada".

def: A person's point of view on life, or the general prospect for the future.
ex: Despite recent layoffs, the general industry outlook for cybersecurity professionals remains extremely positive.
nat: Traveling alone across Southeast Asia gave him a much broader outlook on international cultures.

mis.bad: His outlook of life changed completely.
mis.good: His outlook on life changed completely.
mis.why: Always use "outlook on [life/things]", never "outlook of".

def: To perform better than another person, company, or technical benchmark.
ex: Our newly optimized Rust backend managed to outperform the previous Python service by threefold.
nat: Value stocks rarely outperform technology shares during extended periods of low interest rates.

mis.bad: The app outperformed than the competitor.
mis.good: The app outperformed the competitor.
mis.why: "Outperform" is transitive; do not insert "than".

def: An extremely strong reaction of anger, shock, or indignation.
ex: The sudden cancellation of train service provoked widespread passenger outrage during rush hour.
nat: News of the bribery scandal caused moral outrage across the entire international community.

mis.bad: He felt an outrage about the news.
mis.good: He felt outrage at the news.
mis.why: "Outrage" is usually uncountable here; say "felt outrage at" rather than "an outrage about".

def: Shockingly bad or excessive; completely unacceptable in price or behavior.
ex: Charging fifty dollars for basic hotel Wi-Fi is an absolutely outrageous business practice.
nat: The tabloids published outrageous rumors that damaged the diplomat professional standing.

mis.bad: The hotel price was very outrage.
mis.good: The hotel price was outrageous.
mis.why: Use the adjective "outrageous" rather than the noun "outrage" to describe prices or actions.

def: Immediately, entirely, or without reservation or hesitation.
ex: The CEO rejected the buyout proposal outright during the opening ten minutes of discussions.
nat: Instead of leasing equipment, the company chose to purchase the delivery vans outright.

mis.bad: He refused outrightly to sign the contract.
mis.good: He refused outright to sign the contract.
mis.why: "Outright" is already an adverb; do not say "outrightly".

pt: passar a perna com esperteza / ser mais esperto que
def: To defeat or get the better of someone by being cleverer.
ex: Skilled penetration testers routinely outsmart automated scanners by crafting unique custom exploit chains.
nat: The clever detective managed to outsmart the criminal at every single tactical turn.

mis.bad: He outsmarted to his rivals.
mis.good: He outsmarted his rivals.
mis.why: "Outsmart" is a direct transitive verb; do not add "to".

pt: ultrapassar / superar em ritmo ou quantidade
def: To move faster than and overtake someone, or exceed in quantity.
ex: Consumer demand for electric vehicles began to outstrip supply chain factory production capabilities.
nat: Inflationary pressures quickly outstrip wage increases when central banks fail to act decisively.

mis.bad: Demand outstripped over production.
mis.good: Demand outstripped production.
mis.why: "Outstrip" takes a direct object without prepositions like "over".

def: Of or relating to the outside or outer surface; apparent to observers.
ex: Despite severe internal turbulence, the executive maintained an outward appearance of calm confidence.
nat: The company outward image masked deep organizational dysfunction and growing employee turnover.

mis.bad: His outwardly appearance was calm.
mis.good: His outward appearance was calm.
mis.why: Use the adjective "outward" before nouns ("outward appearance"), reserving "outwardly" for adverbs.

pt: superar em peso / ter mais relevância que
def: To be greater or more significant than something else in comparison.
ex: The long-term productivity advantages of automated testing far outweigh the initial onboarding costs.
nat: Do the potential rewards of moving abroad outweigh the difficulty of leaving family?

mis.bad: The benefits outweigh over the costs.
mis.good: The benefits outweigh the costs.
mis.why: "Outweigh" is transitive; do not use "over" or "than".

pt: da noite para o dia / durante a noite
def: For or during the night, or suddenly and unexpectedly.
ex: Do not expect your conversational English fluency to transform miraculously overnight without effort.
nat: We left our mobile phones charging overnight on the bedside wooden table.

mis.bad: Success does not come from night to day.
mis.good: Success does not happen overnight.
mis.why: Translate the Portuguese idiom "do dia para a noite" as "overnight", not "from night to day".

def: To use authority to reject or cancel a decision; or take precedence over.
ex: System administrators can override standard access permissions in case of a critical security breach.
nat: Local configuration variables usually override default global settings in modern software frameworks.

mis.bad: The manager overridden the decision.
mis.good: The manager overrode the decision.
mis.why: The past tense of "override" is "overrode"; the past participle is "overridden".

def: To reject or disallow by exercising higher authority.
ex: The judge decided to overrule the defense attorney objection during the morning trial session.
nat: The company board voted to overrule the CEO proposed merger proposal yesterday.

mis.bad: The court overruled down the request.
mis.good: The court overruled the request.
mis.why: "Overrule" does not take "down"; use "overrule + object" directly.

def: To go beyond an expected limit or budget, or spread over rapidly.
ex: Poor milestone planning caused the construction project to overrun its initial budget by millions.
nat: Weeds will quickly overrun the vegetable garden if you stop weeding every weekend.

mis.bad: The project overrunned the budget.
mis.good: The project overran the budget.
mis.why: The past tense of "overrun" is "overran"; the past participle is "overrun".

def: To catch up with and pass while traveling in the same direction.
ex: Never attempt to overtake a heavy cargo truck on a narrow mountain curve.
nat: Renewable electricity generation is projected to overtake coal output within the next three years.

mis.bad: He overtooked the car on the right.
mis.good: He overtook the car on the right.
mis.why: The irregular past tense of "overtake" is "overtook", not "overtooked".

def: To tip over or reverse an existing legal decision or political verdict.
ex: The appellate court moved to overturn the lower court ruling regarding software copyright protection.
nat: Strong coastal winds caused an empty delivery van to overturn on the suspension bridge.

mis.bad: The supreme court overturned to the ban.
mis.good: The supreme court overturned the ban.
mis.why: "Overturn" is transitive; do not insert "to" before the object.

def: The speed at which someone walks, runs, or at which something develops.
ex: Studying vocabulary at a consistent daily pace produces far better results than weekend cramming.
nat: The rapid pace of technological change demands continuous upskilling from software professionals.

mis.bad: I cannot follow the pace of the teacher.
mis.good: I cannot keep pace with the teacher.
mis.why: The common idiom is "keep pace with [someone]", not "follow the pace".

def: Completely full of people or things; crowded.
ex: The morning commuter train was so packed that several passengers could not board.
nat: The festival organizers announced that Saturday evening tickets were completely packed out.

mis.bad: The conference room was packed of people.
mis.good: The conference room was packed with people.
mis.why: Always use "packed with [people/things]", never "packed of".

def: Affected with or causing physical pain, or causing severe mental distress.
ex: Stretching a strained muscle too aggressively can be extremely painful and counterproductive.
nat: Making the decision to shut down the startup was a painful experience for everyone.

mis.bad: My foot is very pain.
mis.good: My foot is very painful / hurts a lot.
mis.why: Use the adjective "painful" or the verb "hurts", not the noun "pain".

def: Causing no physical pain, or involving little difficulty or effort.
ex: The automated migration script made transferring database records completely painless for the team.
nat: Modern dental techniques ensure that routine cavity fillings are virtually painless today.

mis.bad: The process was painless of problems.
mis.good: The process was painless and trouble-free.
mis.why: "Painless" does not take "of"; use it alone or with coordinating adjectives.

pt: paleta de cores / conjunto de opções
def: A range of colors used by an artist, or available in software design.
ex: The design system uses a muted color palette to reduce visual fatigue for users.
nat: The chef combined unusual citrus flavors to expand the culinary palette of the menu.

mis.bad: Change the pallete on the CSS file.
mis.good: Change the palette in the CSS file.
mis.why: Note the spelling: "palette" (colors) vs. "palate" (roof of mouth/taste) vs. "pallet" (wooden platform).

def: Feeling or characterized by sudden, overwhelming fear or anxiety.
ex: Try to stay calm and avoid making panicky decisions when production monitoring alarms trigger.
nat: Investors grew panicky when the stock plunged ten percent within two trading minutes.

mis.bad: He became panic when the server stopped.
mis.good: He grew panicky when the server stopped.
mis.why: Use the adjective "panicky" (or "panicked") after linking verbs like "became" or "grew".

def: Side by side and having the same distance continuously between them; corresponding.
ex: Distributed systems execute tasks across parallel computing threads to maximize hardware utilization.
nat: The author drew an interesting parallel between the Roman collapse and modern economic challenges.

mis.bad: The processes run in parallel with each other.
mis.good: The processes run in parallel.
mis.why: Say "run in parallel", dropping "with each other" when understood.

def: To cause a person or part of the body to lose function; halt activity completely.
ex: A widespread ransomware infection can paralyze hospital operations and prevent emergency admissions.
nat: Fear of public failure should never paralyze your ambition to lead new initiatives.

mis.bad: The incident paralised the company network.
mis.good: The incident paralyzed the company network.
mis.why: American English spelling prefers "paralyze" with a "z".

def: More important than anything else; supreme in status or significance.
ex: Protecting confidential customer payment data is of paramount importance to our engineering organization.
nat: Maintaining clean drinking water supply is paramount during humanitarian emergency relief operations.

mis.bad: Safety is in paramount importance.
mis.good: Safety is of paramount importance.
mis.why: The fixed phrase is "of paramount importance", never "in".

def: Characterized by unreasonable suspicion and mistrust of other people.
ex: Good security engineers are slightly paranoid about verifying all incoming network packet signatures.
nat: He became paranoid that coworkers were secretly undermining his promotion prospects.

mis.bad: She is paranoid with her privacy.
mis.good: She is paranoid about her privacy.
mis.why: Use "paranoid about [something]", not "with".

def: To analyze a string or text into its component parts of speech or syntax.
ex: The frontend application must parse the incoming JSON response before updating the view model.
nat: Our backend script parses gigabytes of server log files in under five seconds.

mis.bad: The function cannot parse to the date.
mis.good: The function cannot parse the date.
mis.why: "Parse" is directly transitive; do not insert "to".

def: Only in part; to a limited extent or degree.
ex: The old airport terminal was partially demolished to make room for a new runway.
nat: Our team has only partially implemented the new authentication protocol so far.

mis.bad: I partially agree with you.
mis.good: I partly agree with you / partially agree with you.
mis.why: Both "partly" and "partially" work, but avoid "in part of" where an adverb belongs.

def: A person who takes part in something or participates in an event.
ex: Each participant in the user testing study received a fifty-dollar digital gift card.
nat: The workshop had thirty active participants representing five different South American countries.

mis.bad: Every participants signed the sheet.
mis.good: Every participant signed the sheet.
mis.why: "Every" must be followed by a singular noun: "every participant".

def: To take part in an action or event with others.
ex: All engineers are warmly encouraged to participate in weekly open-source code review sessions.
nat: Did you participate in the community hackathon that happened last weekend?

mis.bad: I want to participate of the hackathon.
mis.good: I want to participate in the hackathon.
mis.why: Always use "participate in", never "participate of" (calque of Portuguese "participar de").

def: A minute portion of matter, or a very small piece of something.
ex: The high-efficiency HEPA air filter traps ninety-nine percent of microscopic dust particles.
nat: Physicists at the laboratory accelerated subatomic particles to nearly the speed of light.

mis.bad: There was not a particle of true in his statement.
mis.good: There was not a particle of truth in his statement.
mis.why: Use the noun "truth" after "particle of", not the adjective "true".

def: Prejudiced in favor of a particular cause or political party.
ex: The news outlet faced severe criticism for publishing blatantly partisan election coverage.
nat: Passing significant infrastructure legislation requires genuine bipartisan compromise rather than partisan bickering.

mis.bad: The debate became very partidar.
mis.good: The debate became very partisan.
mis.why: The English adjective is "partisan", not "partidar".

def: An association of two or more people or organizations as partners.
ex: The university announced a strategic research partnership with a leading quantum computing startup.
nat: Working in close partnership with our UX designer helped speed up feature delivery.

mis.bad: We made a partnership with them.
mis.good: We formed a partnership with them.
mis.why: Use "form / enter into a partnership", not "make a partnership".

def: A short section of a written work, or a narrow corridor or way through.
ex: The exam asks candidates to read a complex technical passage and answer questions.
nat: A narrow secret passage connected the wine cellar to the castle main hall.

mis.bad: I bought a passage of plane to Miami.
mis.good: I bought a plane ticket to Miami.
mis.why: For travel tickets, use "ticket", not "passage" (which refers to corridors or excerpts).

def: Showing or caused by strong feelings or a strong belief in something.
ex: She is deeply passionate about mentoring young women pursuing careers in software engineering.
nat: The speaker gave a passionate presentation that brought the entire audience to tears.

mis.bad: He is passionate for photography.
mis.good: He is passionate about photography.
mis.why: Always use "passionate about [something]", not "passionate for".

def: The capacity to accept or tolerate delay, trouble, or suffering without getting angry.
ex: Teaching junior developers complex distributed systems concepts requires an enormous amount of patience.
nat: My patience wore thin after waiting on hold for forty-five minutes with airline support.

mis.bad: He does not have much pacience.
mis.good: He does not have much patience.
mis.why: Spell "patience" with "ti", not "ci" (calque of Portuguese "paciência").

def: A customer, especially a regular one, or a financial supporter of arts/causes.
ex: The neighborhood cafe rewarded loyal patrons with a complimentary cup on Friday mornings.
nat: The Renaissance artist relied on wealthy patrons to finance his monumental oil paintings.

mis.bad: He is a patron of this store (meaning boss).
mis.good: He is the owner of this store.
mis.why: False friend: "patron" in English means a customer or benefactor, not the owner/boss ("boss" or "owner").

def: The support given by a patron, or the regular business given to a store.
ex: The small independent bookstore survived pandemic restrictions thanks to generous local community patronage.
nat: Royal patronage allowed astronomers during the seventeenth century to build advanced observation telescopes.

mis.bad: We thank you by your patronage.
mis.good: We thank you for your patronage.
mis.why: Use "thank you for [something]", not "thank you by".

def: To treat someone with an apparent kindness that betrays a feeling of superiority.
ex: Do not patronize junior engineers when explaining fundamental networking principles in team channels.
nat: We chose to patronize independent local bakeries instead of corporate supermarket chains.

mis.bad: He patronized about me.
mis.good: He patronized me.
mis.why: "Patronize" is directly transitive; omit prepositions like "about".

def: To stop temporarily doing something or speaking before continuing.
ex: Let us pause the video tutorial here so everyone can configure their local settings.
nat: She paused for a brief moment before answering the tough interviewer question.

mis.bad: I paused to write the message.
mis.good: I paused to read the message.
mis.why: Be careful: "pause to + verb" means stop in order to do something.

def: The part of a vehicle load or transmitted data that produces cargo revenue.
ex: The rocket delivered its communications satellite payload into geostationary orbit without any issues.
nat: Make sure the HTTP POST request payload does not exceed five megabytes in size.

mis.bad: The payload from the request was empty.
mis.good: The request payload was empty.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "request payload" or "the payload of the request".

def: The pointed top of a mountain, or the highest point of achievement or activity.
ex: Cloud server capacity must scale automatically during peak holiday online shopping shopping hours.
nat: They reached the mountain peak just as the sunrise illuminated the snowy valley below.

mis.bad: Traffic reached the pike at six.
mis.good: Traffic reached its peak at six.
mis.why: Do not confuse "peak" (ápice) with "pike" (lança/peixe).

def: Strange or odd; unusual; or belonging exclusively to a particular place or person.
ex: The legacy application exhibited peculiar behavior whenever two users updated records at once.
nat: Kangaroo pouch reproduction is peculiar to marsupial mammals native to Australasia.

mis.bad: This dialect is peculiar with this region.
mis.good: This dialect is peculiar to this region.
mis.why: When meaning characteristic of, use "peculiar to", not "with".

def: To succeed in forcing a way into or through something; understand or enter.
ex: Malicious hackers failed to penetrate our internal corporate network thanks to strict firewall segmentation.
nat: The startup struggled to penetrate the competitive Japanese consumer electronics marketplace.

mis.bad: The virus penetrated inside the system.
mis.good: The virus penetrated the system.
mis.why: "Penetrate" already means go inside; avoid redundant adverbs like "inside".

def: Awaiting decision or settlement; or about to happen soon.
ex: Your software deployment is currently pending approval from the lead release engineering coordinator.
nat: Several patent lawsuits remained pending while settlement negotiations proceeded behind closed doors.

mis.bad: My request is in pending.
mis.good: My request is pending.
mis.why: Use "pending" directly as a predicate adjective; do not say "is in pending".

def: Lasting or existing for a long or apparently infinite time; continually recurring.
ex: Managing dependencies and technical debt is a perennial challenge for large engineering organizations.
nat: Lavender is a hardy perennial plant that blossoms beautifully summer after summer.

mis.bad: This is a perennial issue that lasts few days.
mis.good: This is a temporary issue that lasts a few days.
mis.why: "Perennial" implies long-lasting or endlessly recurring, not short-lived.

def: Serious and immediate danger; the risk of harm or loss.
ex: Ignoring software vulnerability alerts places critical hospital infrastructure in grave peril every day.
nat: Sailors faced great peril as monster waves battered their wooden ship at night.

mis.bad: They were in peril of lose everything.
mis.good: They were in peril of losing everything.
mis.why: After the preposition "of", use a gerund: "in peril of losing".

def: The continuous line forming the boundary of a closed geometric figure or area.
ex: Security guards patrol the entire outer perimeter of the data center every two hours.
nat: Calculate the total perimeter of the server room before ordering baseboard cabling tracks.

mis.bad: The perimeter of the circle is its radius.
mis.good: The perimeter of a circle is its circumference.
mis.why: In geometry, the perimeter of a circle is specifically called its "circumference".

def: Appearing or occurring at intervals; happening repeatedly according to a schedule.
ex: Automated backup jobs run at periodic intervals throughout the night without manual intervention.
nat: The chemistry teacher asked students to memorize key elements from the periodic table.

mis.bad: We do periodic checks very sometimes.
mis.good: We perform periodic checks.
mis.why: "Periodic" already conveys regular scheduled occurrence; avoid adding "very sometimes".

def: To die, especially in a violent, sudden, or untimely way; or spoil.
ex: Thousands of farm animals perished during the historic summer drought across the plains.
nat: Without refrigerated shipping containers, fresh dairy products quickly perish on long overseas journeys.

mis.bad: The milk perished on the table yesterday.
mis.good: The milk spoiled on the table yesterday.
mis.why: For food going bad, "spoil" or "go bad" is everyday English; "perish" is formal or poetic.

def: To spread throughout something; pervade every part of an organization or substance.
ex: A culture of continuous learning must permeate the entire engineering team to stay competitive.
nat: The aroma of freshly roasted Ethiopian coffee began to permeate every hallway upstairs.

mis.bad: The smell permeated inside the room.
mis.good: The smell permeated the room.
mis.why: "Permeate" is transitive; do not add "inside".

def: At an angle of ninety degrees to a given line, plane, or surface.
ex: The vertical support beam must be exactly perpendicular to the horizontal foundation slab.
nat: Turn right onto the street that runs perpendicular to the main shopping avenue.

mis.bad: The wall is perpendicular with the floor.
mis.good: The wall is perpendicular to the floor.
mis.why: Always use "perpendicular to", never "perpendicular with".

def: To make something, typically an undesirable situation or unfounded belief, continue indefinitely.
ex: Biased hiring algorithms can unintentionally perpetuate existing gender imbalances within technical leadership roles.
nat: Spreading unverified rumors online only serves to perpetuate public anxiety and panic needlessly.

mis.bad: The news perpetuates on the stereotype.
mis.good: The news perpetuates the stereotype.
mis.why: "Perpetuate" takes a direct object without prepositions like "on".

def: To cause someone to feel completely baffled or puzzled; confuse thoroughly.
ex: The strange intermittent memory leak continued to perplex senior systems engineers for weeks.
nat: Cryptic tax regulation instructions never fail to perplex first-time independent freelance consultants.

mis.bad: I was very perplex with the error.
mis.good: I was very perplexed by the error.
mis.why: Use the participle "perplexed" with "by" to describe how a person feels.

def: To continue in a course of action even in the face of difficulty.
ex: Learners who persevere through initial conversational frustration invariably attain solid professional English fluency.
nat: Despite repeated hardware prototype rejections, the inventor chose to persevere with his dream.

mis.bad: She persevered in study English.
mis.good: She persevered in studying English.
mis.why: After the preposition "in", always use the gerund: "persevered in studying".

def: Continuing firmly in a course of action; or continuing to exist stubbornly.
ex: He finally found the solution thanks to persistent debugging throughout the entire weekend.
nat: A persistent dry cough after a respiratory infection requires a visit to your doctor.

mis.bad: She was persistent to finish the book.
mis.good: She was persistent in finishing the book.
mis.why: Use "persistent in + -ing", not "persistent to + base verb".

def: The combination of characteristics or qualities that form an individual distinctive character.
ex: Her warm and approachable personality makes new engineering recruits feel instantly welcome here.
nat: Different personality traits can influence whether someone thrives in remote or office environments.

mis.bad: He has a good personalty.
mis.good: He has a pleasant personality.
mis.why: Spell "personality" with six syllables and "al-i-ty", not "personalty" (which means movable property in legal contexts).

pt: duto / esteira de automação ou vendas
def: A pipe used to transport liquids; or a channel through which products/code pass.
ex: The continuous integration pipeline automatically runs unit tests whenever code is pushed upstream.
nat: Our commercial sales pipeline currently includes eight enterprise prospects ready for contract review.

mis.bad: We have three new features on the pipeline.
mis.good: We have three new features in the pipeline.
mis.why: The fixed preposition is "in the pipeline", never "on".

def: To find or locate the exact place, time, or cause of something.
ex: Profiling tools helped developers pinpoint the exact database query causing severe dashboard slowdowns.
nat: It is difficult to pinpoint the moment when user growth turned into viral adoption.

mis.bad: We pinpointed to the problem.
mis.good: We pinpointed the problem.
mis.why: "Pinpoint" is directly transitive; omit "to".

def: A person who is among the first to explore or develop a new area.
ex: Grace Hopper was a true computing pioneer who championed machine-independent programming languages.
nat: Early renewable energy pioneers proved that utility-scale wind power could be commercially profitable.

mis.bad: He is a pioneer of artificial intelligence.
mis.good: He is a pioneer in artificial intelligence.
mis.why: Use "pioneer in [a field]", not "pioneer of".

def: Devoutly religious, or making a hypocritical display of virtue.
ex: Behind his pious public speeches lay a ruthless ambition to enrich himself through embezzlement.
nat: The monastery was founded by pious monks seeking quiet contemplation in the mountains.

mis.bad: He gave a pious advise.
mis.good: He gave pious advice.
